title: Dependency Inversion
statementMd:
Luisa Lopes is studying for her Software Engineering exam and has gotten stuck on the SOLID principles, which underpin the course.

![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/37b35848a7e519847f9d069fc2afe8981fffcd79.png)

To help the ideas sink in, she decides to examine the dependency graph of a legacy project she maintains as a freelancer. Each vertex represents a module, and a directed edge from 𝑢u to 𝑣v means that module 𝑢u depends directly on module 𝑣v. A well-designed project should have no cyclic dependencies: no module should depend, directly or indirectly, on itself. Luisa suspects that her project has exactly this problem.

Thinking about the "D" in SOLID, the *Dependency Inversion Principle*, she starts wondering about reversing dependencies. Could reversing a single dependency eliminate all the cycles at once?

With little time left before her exam, Luisa asks for your help. Given a directed graph 𝐺G, determine whether it can be made acyclic by reversing **at most one** edge. Reversing an edge 𝑢→𝑣u→v means replacing it with 𝑣→𝑢v→u.

## Input

The first line contains an integer 𝑡t (1≤𝑡≤2×1051≤t≤2×105), the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains two integers 𝑛n and 𝑚m (1≤𝑛≤2×1051≤n≤2×105, 0≤𝑚≤min(3×105,𝑛(𝑛−1)/2)0≤m≤min(3×105,n(n−1)/2)), the numbers of vertices and directed edges.

Each of the next 𝑚m lines contains two integers 𝑢u and 𝑣v (1≤𝑢,𝑣≤𝑛1≤u,v≤n, 𝑢≠𝑣u≠v), describing a directed edge from 𝑢u to 𝑣v. For each unordered pair of vertices {𝑢,𝑣}{u,v}, there is at most one edge between them.

The sum of 𝑛n over all test cases does not exceed 2×1052×105, and the sum of 𝑚m does not exceed 3×1053×105.

## Output

For each test case, print on the first line: `0` if the graph is already acyclic; `1` if it is not acyclic but reversing one edge can make it acyclic; or `-1` otherwise.

If you print `1`, print a second line containing two integers 𝑢u and 𝑣v, identifying an edge 𝑢→𝑣u→v whose reversal makes the graph acyclic. Any such edge is accepted. Print its endpoints in their **original input order**.

## Note

**Explanation for example 1**

In the first example, reversing edge 1→21→2 breaks the only cycle, so printing `1` followed by `1 2` is accepted. Any other edge whose reversal makes the graph acyclic would also be accepted.

**Explanation for example 2**

Here, the graph is not acyclic, and reversing one edge cannot make it acyclic. The expected output is therefore `-1`.
